1.summary: Zechariah calls the people to return to God unlike their fathers, then sees night visions of patrolling horsemen and of four horns cast down, promising that God has returned to Jerusalem with mercy.
1.lookfor: Notice the call to return in 1:3, the question how long? in 1:12, and the way each vision is explained by an angel.

names.name: Zechariah
names.gloss: The prophet; his name means Yahweh remembers.

names.name: Berechiah
names.gloss: Zechariah's father.

names.name: Iddo
names.gloss: Zechariah's grandfather, head of a priestly family that returned from Babylon.

names.name: Darius
names.gloss: Darius I, king of Persia from 522 to 486 BC.

insights.title: Return to me
insights.body: Return to me, and I will return to you (1:3). Zechariah begins where the former prophets ended: their call to repent was ignored, and their words overtook the fathers (1:4-6). Malachi uses the same promise a century later.

insights.title: Where are they now?
insights.body: Your fathers, where are they? And the prophets, do they live forever? (1:5). Both the people and the prophets have died, but God's word has outlived them and come true. The words of God last when human messengers pass away.

insights.title: Eight visions in one night
insights.body: On a single night in February 519 BC (1:7), Zechariah receives eight visions that run to 6:8. They are full of symbols and explained by an interpreting angel, a feature of the apocalyptic writing that develops in Daniel and Revelation.

insights.title: God's patrol
insights.body: Horsemen patrol the earth and report that all is at rest (1:10-11). The Persian king was famous for his network of mounted couriers and informants, sometimes called the eyes of the king. Zechariah pictures God with his own scouts, though their report of a world at ease is not good news for Judah.

insights.title: Seventy years
insights.body: The angel asks, How long? ... these seventy years (1:12), recalling Jeremiah's prophecy. From the temple's destruction in 586 BC to 519 BC was about sixty-seven years, and the temple was finished in 515 BC, almost exactly seventy years later.

insights.title: A little displeased
insights.body: God says he was only a little displeased with his people, but the nations added to the calamity (1:15). The empires that punished Judah went far beyond what God intended. God's anger now turns against them, and his mercy toward Jerusalem.

insights.title: Horns and craftsmen
insights.body: The four horns are the powers that scattered God's people (1:19), and the four craftsmen or smiths come to break them (1:21). Horns stood for strength; four suggests every direction. In Hebrew Bibles 1:18-21 are counted as 2:1-4.

insights.title: Kind and comforting words
insights.body: To the angel's question, God answers with kind and comforting words (1:13). After seventy years of judgment, the first thing God says is comfort. What does it suggest that comfort comes before the rebuilding has even begun?

2.summary: In the third vision a man measuring Jerusalem is told the city will overflow without walls, protected by God as a wall of fire; the exiles are called home, and many nations will join themselves to Yahweh.
2.lookfor: Notice why the city will have no walls, the call to flee Babylon, and the promise about the nations in 2:11.

names.name: Babylon
names.gloss: The city and region where many Jews still lived after the return began.

insights.title: No need for walls
insights.body: A young man goes to measure Jerusalem, perhaps planning walls, but is told the city will be like open villages because of its many people and animals (2:4). Jerusalem was then small and its walls in ruins. Nehemiah later rebuilt the walls, but Zechariah envisions a city whose security rests on God.

insights.title: A wall of fire
insights.body: God will be a wall of fire around the city and the glory in the middle of her (2:5). The pillar of fire led and protected Israel in the wilderness, and Ezekiel saw God's glory leave the temple before its destruction. Now the glory returns.

insights.title: Flee from the north
insights.body: Come! Flee from the land of the north (2:6) urges Jews still in Babylon to return. Many exiles had settled comfortably and stayed. Babylon had twice revolted against Darius and been crushed shortly before, which made the call more urgent.

insights.title: The apple of his eye
insights.body: He who touches you touches the apple of his eye (2:8). The Hebrew probably refers to the pupil, the most sensitive and protected part of the eye. Deuteronomy uses a similar phrase for God's care for Israel in the wilderness.

insights.title: Many nations
insights.body: Many nations shall join themselves to Yahweh in that day, and shall be my people (2:11). The covenant phrase my people, once for Israel alone, is extended to the nations. It continues the promise to Abraham that all families would be blessed.

insights.title: The holy land
insights.body: Yahweh will inherit Judah as his portion in the holy land (2:12). This is the only place in the Bible where the land of Israel is called the holy land, a phrase later common in Jewish and Christian usage. It is holy because God dwells there.

insights.title: Sing and rejoice
insights.body: Sing and rejoice, daughter of Zion; for, behold, I come, and I will dwell within you (2:10). Zephaniah and later Zechariah 9 use similar calls to rejoice. John's Gospel says the Word dwelt, literally pitched his tent, among us.

insights.title: Be silent, all flesh
insights.body: The chapter ends: Be silent, all flesh, before Yahweh; for he has roused himself (2:13). Habakkuk and Zephaniah use the same call to silence. What kind of silence is fitting when God is about to act?

3.summary: In the fourth vision the high priest Joshua stands accused by Satan in filthy clothes, but God rebukes the accuser, clothes Joshua in clean garments, and promises his servant the Branch.
3.lookfor: Notice who speaks for Joshua, what happens to his clothes, and the promises about the Branch and the stone.

names.name: Joshua
names.gloss: The high priest of the returned community.

names.name: Satan
names.gloss: In Hebrew the satan, the accuser or adversary, standing in the heavenly court.

insights.title: A courtroom in heaven
insights.body: Joshua stands before Yahweh's angel with Satan at his right hand to accuse him (3:1), the position of a prosecutor. As in Job, the satan is an accuser in the heavenly court. Here he accuses the high priest, who represents the whole people.

insights.title: Yahweh rebuke you
insights.body: Yahweh rebuke you, Satan! (3:2). Jude says the archangel Michael used these words when disputing with the devil about the body of Moses. Joshua is a burning stick plucked from the fire: snatched from the fire of exile, as Amos said of Israel.

insights.title: Filthy garments
insights.body: Joshua is dressed in filthy garments (3:3). The Hebrew word is unusually strong, linked to the word for excrement. The high priest was required to wear clean holy garments; filth symbolises the guilt of priest and people after exile.

insights.title: Clean clothes and a turban
insights.body: God has the filthy clothes removed and rich clothing put on (3:4). Zechariah himself interrupts to ask for a clean turban (3:5), the headdress that bore the gold plate engraved Holy to Yahweh. Christian readers have seen here a picture of forgiveness as being clothed by God.

insights.title: My servant, the Branch
insights.body: God will bring my servant, the Branch (3:8). Jeremiah had promised a righteous Branch for David, a new king from David's family tree. Jewish and Christian interpreters have read the Branch as the Messiah; in Zechariah's day many saw it in Zerubbabel.

insights.title: A stone with seven eyes
insights.body: God sets a stone before Joshua with seven eyes, and will remove the land's iniquity in one day (3:9). The stone may be a foundation stone of the temple, or a jewel on the high priest's clothing; the seven eyes may be facets or God's watchful eyes (4:10). Its exact meaning is debated.

insights.title: A priesthood restored
insights.body: Joshua is promised access to God's courts if he walks in God's ways (3:7). After exile, with no king, the high priest became the main leader of the Jewish community. The vision affirms that the priesthood, stained by exile, is cleansed and accepted.

insights.title: In one day
insights.body: God will remove the iniquity of that land in one day (3:9). The Day of Atonement removed sins once a year. Christians have connected this with Christ's death, which Hebrews calls a single offering. How might a whole land's guilt be removed in a day?

4.summary: In the fifth vision Zechariah sees a golden lampstand fed by two olive trees, and hears that Zerubbabel will finish the temple not by might nor by power but by God's Spirit.
4.lookfor: Notice the famous word to Zerubbabel in 4:6, the question about small things, and who the two olive trees represent.

names.name: Zerubbabel
names.gloss: The governor of Judah from David's royal line, leading the rebuilding.

insights.title: A golden lampstand
insights.body: The lampstand has a bowl on top and seven lamps, each with channels for wicks (4:2). It recalls the seven-branched menorah of the tabernacle, though its design differs. Oil flows straight from the trees, so no human has to fill it.

insights.title: Not by might, nor by power
insights.body: Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit (4:6). Zerubbabel had no army or wealth to rely on, only a small community under Persian rule. Zechariah 2:14–4:7 in the Hebrew numbering is read in synagogues on the Sabbath of Hanukkah, which celebrates the temple's rededication.

insights.title: Who are you, great mountain?
insights.body: Who are you, great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you are a plain (4:7). The obstacles to rebuilding, whether opposition, poverty or discouragement, will be levelled. Jesus spoke of faith that could move mountains.

insights.title: The capstone
insights.body: Zerubbabel will bring out the capstone with shouts of Grace, grace, to it! (4:7). Ancient building ceremonies marked the placing of key stones. The stone may be the final top stone or a stone from the old temple placed in the new.

insights.title: The day of small things
insights.body: Who despises the day of small things? (4:10). The new temple seemed tiny compared to Solomon's. The question has encouraged many who start something modest. Why might small beginnings matter to God?

insights.title: Two sons of oil
insights.body: The two olive trees are the two anointed ones (4:14), literally two sons of oil. Most interpreters see Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the priest, two leaders working together. Revelation calls its two witnesses the two olive trees and the two lampstands.

insights.title: The eyes of Yahweh
insights.body: The seven lamps are Yahweh's eyes, which run back and forth through the whole earth (4:10). Chronicles uses almost the same words. God sees everything, including the small beginnings at Jerusalem.

insights.title: His hands shall finish it
insights.body: The hands of Zerubbabel laid the foundation, and his hands shall also finish it (4:9). The temple was completed in 515 BC, within Zerubbabel's lifetime. The promise came true, which Zechariah says will prove he was sent by God.

5.summary: In the sixth and seventh visions, a huge flying scroll brings God's curse on thieves and perjurers, and a woman named Wickedness is shut in a basket and carried off to Babylonia.
5.lookfor: Notice the size of the scroll, the two sins it names, and where the basket is taken.

names.name: Shinar
names.gloss: An old name for Babylonia, where the tower of Babel was built.

insights.title: A giant flying scroll
insights.body: The scroll is twenty cubits by ten, about nine by four and a half metres (5:2). These are the dimensions of the porch of Solomon's temple. A scroll that size, unrolled and flying, would be visible to all.

insights.title: Theft and false oaths
insights.body: The curse falls on everyone who steals and everyone who swears falsely by God's name (5:3-4). These represent both tables of the Ten Commandments: sins against neighbours and against God. The rebuilding of the temple must be matched by a cleansing of society.

insights.title: The curse enters the house
insights.body: The curse enters the house of the thief and lodges there until it destroys it, timber and stones (5:4). Unlike a law that waits for a court, God's word itself carries out the sentence. It recalls the treatment of a house with spreading mould in Leviticus.

insights.title: An ephah basket
insights.body: An ephah was a dry measure of about twenty litres, and the ephah basket (5:6) was the container used to measure grain. A woman inside is called Wickedness (5:8), and a lead cover is clamped on. Some see a link to dishonest measures in trade.

insights.title: Wings like a stork
insights.body: Two women with wings like a stork carry the basket away (5:9). The stork was an unclean bird under the law, which may fit the task of removing wickedness. The wind in their wings suggests God's spirit carrying it off.

insights.title: Back to Shinar
insights.body: Wickedness is taken to the land of Shinar, where a house will be built for her (5:11). Shinar is the land of Babel, the city of human pride. Revelation pictures Babylon as a woman embodying the world's evil.

insights.title: Holiness for the land
insights.body: Visions 6 and 7 deal with sin, not with buildings or politics. A renewed temple needs a renewed people. Evil is removed from God's land rather than merely punished within it.

insights.title: A house for wickedness
insights.body: Wickedness gets a temple of her own in Babylon, set on her base (5:11), a dark parody of the temple being built in Jerusalem. What does the vision suggest about where evil belongs and where it does not?

6.summary: In the eighth vision four chariots go out from between bronze mountains to patrol the earth; then Zechariah is told to make crowns from the exiles' gifts and set them on the high priest Joshua, announcing the Branch who will build the temple.
6.lookfor: Compare the chariots with the horsemen of chapter 1, and notice who receives the crown and what is said of the Branch.

names.name: Heldai
names.gloss: A returned exile who brought gifts from Babylon; also called Helem.

names.name: Tobijah
names.gloss: A returned exile who brought gifts.

names.name: Jedaiah
names.gloss: A returned exile, perhaps of a priestly family.

names.name: Josiah
names.gloss: Son of Zephaniah, in whose house the returned exiles stayed.

names.name: Jehozadak
names.gloss: Father of the high priest Joshua.

insights.title: Four chariots
insights.body: Four chariots with red, black, white and dappled horses come from between two mountains of bronze (6:1-3). They are the four winds or spirits of heaven sent through the earth (6:5). The night visions end as they began with horses, now sent out with power. Revelation's four horsemen draw on these images.

insights.title: Quieted my spirit in the north
insights.body: The chariots going north have quieted my spirit in the north country (6:8). The north was where Babylon's armies had come from. God's anger against Babylon is now at rest, perhaps because judgment has been carried out.

insights.title: Gifts from Babylon
insights.body: Heldai, Tobijah and Jedaiah had brought silver and gold from the Jewish community still in Babylon (6:10). Exiles who stayed behind supported the work in Jerusalem, as they had when Cyrus first allowed the return.

insights.title: A crown for the priest
insights.body: Zechariah is told to make crowns and set them on Joshua the high priest (6:11), yet the words that follow speak of the Branch, who seemed to be Zerubbabel. Many scholars think the passage first involved both leaders, with the counsel of peace between them both (6:13), and that it was later focused on the priest as Zerubbabel disappears from history. Others take it as a symbolic act pointing to a future figure.

insights.title: The man whose name is the Branch
insights.body: Behold, the man whose name is the Branch ... he shall build Yahweh's temple (6:12). Jewish tradition reads the Branch as the Messiah. Christians have seen Jesus, who spoke of his body as the temple, as both priest and king.

insights.title: A priest on his throne
insights.body: He shall be a priest on his throne (6:13). In Israel the roles of king and priest were normally separate, and kings who tried to act as priests were judged. A priest-king appears in Melchizedek and in Psalm 110, which Hebrews applies to Christ.

insights.title: A memorial in the temple
insights.body: The crowns were to be kept in the temple as a memorial to the donors (6:14). They would remind future worshippers of the promise of the Branch. Those who are far off will come and help build (6:15).

insights.title: If you obey
insights.body: The chapter ends with a condition: This will happen, if you will diligently obey Yahweh your God's voice (6:15). The great promises depend on a faithful people. How do God's promises and human response fit together here?

7.summary: When people from Bethel ask whether they should keep fasting for the temple's destruction, Zechariah asks whether their fasts were really for God, and reminds them of the former prophets' call to justice and mercy that their fathers ignored.
7.lookfor: Notice the question the delegation asks, the question God asks back, and the four kinds of vulnerable people named in 7:10.

names.name: Bethel
names.gloss: A town north of Jerusalem, once a royal sanctuary of the northern kingdom.

names.name: Sharezer
names.gloss: A member of the delegation, with a Babylonian name.

names.name: Regem Melech
names.gloss: Another delegate; the name may be a title, the king's friend.

insights.title: Should we keep fasting?
insights.body: Two years after the night visions (7:1), people ask whether to keep weeping in the fifth month (7:3), when the temple had been burned. Now the temple is being rebuilt. Should the mourning stop? The answer comes in stages through chapters 7 and 8.

insights.title: Fasts of the exile
insights.body: Jews kept fasts in the fifth month for the temple's destruction and in the seventh for the murder of Gedaliah, the governor after Jerusalem's fall (7:5). These fasts are still observed in Jewish tradition, as Tisha b'Av and the Fast of Gedaliah.

insights.title: Did you fast to me?
insights.body: God answers with his own question: did you at all fast to me, really to me? (7:5). Their fasting, like their eating, was for themselves (7:6). Isaiah also criticises fasting that ignores justice.

insights.title: True judgment and kindness
insights.body: Execute true judgment, and show kindness and compassion every man to his brother (7:9). Don't oppress the widow, fatherless, foreigner or poor (7:10). This summary of the former prophets' message echoes Micah and Amos and the laws of Exodus and Deuteronomy.

insights.title: Hearts like flint
insights.body: They made their hearts as hard as flint (7:12). The Hebrew word, shamir, may mean diamond or emery, the hardest known stone. Ezekiel uses it for the prophet's forehead, made harder than the people's stubbornness.

insights.title: As he called
insights.body: As he called, and they refused to listen, so they will call, and I will not listen (7:13). God's justice mirrors their response. The words recall Proverbs on wisdom calling and being ignored.

insights.title: The former prophets
insights.body: Zechariah refers to the former prophets (7:7, 7:12), the pre-exilic prophets whose words were by then written and collected. He treats their message as authoritative Scripture, sent by God's Spirit. The idea of a body of prophetic writings is taking shape.

insights.title: Ritual or relationship
insights.body: The question about fasting is answered not with a ruling about ritual but with a call to justice and mercy. Why might God answer a religious question with an ethical one? Jesus did the same when asked about sabbath and purity laws.

8.summary: In ten short promises, Yahweh declares he has returned to Zion: old people and children will fill the streets, the remnant will be blessed, fasts will become feasts, and the nations will come seeking God alongside the Jews.
8.lookfor: Count the sayings that begin Yahweh of Armies says, picture the street scene in 8:4-5, and notice what the people must do in 8:16-17.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem, especially the temple hill.

insights.title: Ten promises
insights.body: The chapter is built from about ten short sayings, each opening Yahweh of Armies says (8:2, 8:3, 8:4 and onward). Together they complete the answer to the question about fasting begun in chapter 7. Where chapter 7 looked back at failure, chapter 8 looks forward to blessing.

insights.title: Old people and children
insights.body: Old men and women with walking sticks and children playing in the streets (8:4-5) is a picture of peace and safety. In war, the old and young were the first to die, and a ruined city had neither. A city full of both means generations living out full lives.

insights.title: Too marvellous?
insights.body: If it seems marvellous to the small remnant, should it be marvellous to God? (8:6). The returned community was small and struggling; the promises seemed too good to be true. The question echoes God's word to Abraham: Is anything too hard for Yahweh?

insights.title: A curse becomes a blessing
insights.body: As you were a curse among the nations, so I will save you, and you shall be a blessing (8:13). Exile had made Israel a byword for disaster. The promise recalls God's call of Abraham, that his family would be a blessing to all nations.

insights.title: Truth in the gates
insights.body: The people must speak truth to neighbours and judge with truth and peace in the gates (8:16), with no evil plotting or false oaths (8:17). Paul quotes speak every man the truth with his neighbor in Ephesians. God's promised future requires honest community life now.

insights.title: Four fasts become feasts
insights.body: The fasts of the fourth, fifth, seventh and tenth months (8:19) remembered the breach of Jerusalem's walls, the burning of the temple, Gedaliah's murder and the start of the siege. These fasts are still kept in Jewish tradition. Zechariah promises they will become cheerful feasts.

insights.title: Ten men and a Jew's robe
insights.body: Ten men from every language will take hold of the skirt of a Jew, saying, We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you (8:23). Taking hold of the hem was a gesture of pleading or attachment. The nations come not as conquerors but as seekers.

insights.title: The city of truth
insights.body: Jerusalem will be called The City of Truth (8:3). After centuries of corruption, its new name is about honesty and faithfulness. What would it take for a city or community to earn such a name?

9.summary: A new section announces God's judgment on Israel's neighbours and the coming of Zion's king, humble and riding on a donkey, who will bring peace to the nations and set free the prisoners of hope.
9.lookfor: Notice the nations named in 9:1-7, the description of the king in 9:9, and what he will remove from Israel in 9:10.

names.name: Hadrach
names.gloss: A region in northern Syria, known from Assyrian records as Hatarikka.

names.name: Damascus
names.gloss: Capital of Aram, in Syria.

names.name: Hamath
names.gloss: A city of Syria on the Orontes.

names.name: Tyre
names.gloss: A Phoenician island city, rich from trade.

names.name: Sidon
names.gloss: A Phoenician port north of Tyre.

names.name: Ekron
names.gloss: A Philistine city.

names.name: Jebusite
names.gloss: The people of Jerusalem before David, who were absorbed into Judah.

names.name: Greece
names.gloss: Hebrew Javan, the Greek world.

insights.title: Second Zechariah
insights.body: Chapter 9 begins with A revelation (9:1), the heading also found at 12:1 and Malachi 1:1. The dated visions stop and the style changes to poetry. Many scholars think chapters 9–14 come from a later time; the mention of Greece (9:13) has led some to link chapter 9 with Alexander the Great's march down the coast in 332 BC, when Tyre fell after a famous siege.

insights.title: Philistines as a clan of Judah
insights.body: The Philistines will be stripped of their unclean food and become a remnant for God, like a clan in Judah, and Ekron like the Jebusites (9:7). The Jebusites of Jerusalem had been absorbed into Israel after David took the city. Even old enemies will be included in God's people.

insights.title: Your king comes
insights.body: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion! ... Behold, your King comes to you ... lowly, and riding on a donkey (9:9). Matthew and John quote this verse for Jesus's entry into Jerusalem on Palm Sunday. Jewish tradition also read it of the Messiah; the Talmud contrasts coming on the clouds and coming humbly on a donkey.

insights.title: Why a donkey?
insights.body: Kings rode horses into battle, but a donkey was the mount of peace and of earlier rulers. Solomon rode David's mule to his coronation, and Jacob's blessing pictures Judah's ruler with a donkey's colt. The king of 9:9 comes not with chariots but in humility.

insights.title: No more war horses
insights.body: The king will cut off the chariot and the war horse and the battle bow, and speak peace to the nations (9:10). His rule will reach from sea to sea, the language of Psalm 72. The verse that follows 9:9 makes clear his kingdom is not won by weapons.

insights.title: The blood of your covenant
insights.body: Because of the blood of your covenant, I have set free your prisoners from the waterless pit (9:11). The covenant at Sinai was sealed with blood. Jesus spoke of his blood of the covenant at the Last Supper. A waterless pit was used as a prison, as with Joseph and Jeremiah.

insights.title: Prisoners of hope
insights.body: Turn to the stronghold, you prisoners of hope! (9:12). The phrase suggests people bound not by despair but by hope, held fast by God's promise. God promises to restore double for what they lost.

insights.title: A gentle king and a warrior God
insights.body: The humble king of 9:9-10 is followed by Yahweh as a warrior with bow, arrows and trumpet (9:13-15). How do the two pictures fit together? Many readers see the peace of the king as resting on God's defeat of evil.

10.summary: Yahweh, not idols, gives rain; angry at false shepherds, he will strengthen Judah and Joseph, whistle to gather the scattered people from Egypt and Assyria, and bring them home in a new exodus.
10.lookfor: Notice the contrast between Yahweh and the teraphim, the images of shepherds and the flock, and the echoes of the exodus in 10:10-11.

names.name: Joseph
names.gloss: The northern tribes, especially Ephraim and Manasseh.

names.name: Ephraim
names.gloss: The leading northern tribe, standing for the former northern kingdom.

names.name: Gilead
names.gloss: The hill country east of the Jordan.

names.name: Lebanon
names.gloss: The mountains north of Israel.

insights.title: Ask Yahweh for rain
insights.body: Ask Yahweh for rain in the spring (10:1). The spring or latter rains in March and April were vital for the grain to ripen. Canaanite religion credited Baal with rain; Zechariah insists that Yahweh alone gives it.

insights.title: Teraphim
insights.body: The teraphim (10:2) were household idols used for divination. Rachel stole her father's teraphim, and Michal used one to fool Saul's men. They speak vanity: they cannot guide the people, who wander like sheep without a shepherd.

insights.title: Sheep without a shepherd
insights.body: The people wander like sheep, oppressed because there is no shepherd (10:2). Jesus had compassion on the crowds because they were like sheep without a shepherd. Shepherds in the Bible are often kings and leaders, and Zechariah 9–13 returns to the theme repeatedly.

insights.title: Cornerstone, nail, bow
insights.body: From Judah will come the cornerstone, the tent peg or nail, and the battle bow (10:4), images of stable leaders. The cornerstone holds a building together, and the peg holds up a tent. Isaiah uses the peg image for a reliable leader.

insights.title: North and south reunited
insights.body: God will strengthen Judah and save the house of Joseph (10:6). The northern tribes had been scattered by Assyria two centuries earlier. Zechariah, like Ezekiel, hopes for a reunited Israel.

insights.title: God whistles
insights.body: I will signal for them, and gather them (10:8). The Hebrew verb means to whistle, as a shepherd or beekeeper calls. Isaiah uses the same verb for God whistling up foreign armies; here God whistles his own people home.

insights.title: A new exodus
insights.body: God will bring them out of Egypt and Assyria, through the sea of affliction, drying up the Nile (10:10-11). The language recalls the crossing of the Red Sea. The prophets often pictured the return from exile as a second exodus.

insights.title: Remember me in far countries
insights.body: I will sow them among the peoples, and they will remember me in far countries (10:9). Scattering is described as sowing, a word that holds the promise of growth. How might a people's dispersion turn out to be a kind of planting?

11.summary: The prophet is told to shepherd a flock doomed to slaughter; he breaks his two staffs, Favor and Union, is paid off with thirty pieces of silver which he throws to the potter, and is then told to play the part of a worthless shepherd.
11.lookfor: Notice the names of the two staffs and what happens to each, the wage the prophet receives, and the description of the worthless shepherd.

names.name: Lebanon
names.gloss: Mountains to the north, famous for cedars.

names.name: Bashan
names.gloss: A fertile region east of the Sea of Galilee, known for oaks.

names.name: Jordan
names.gloss: The river valley, whose thickets sheltered lions.

insights.title: Wail, cedars
insights.body: The chapter opens with a taunt: Lebanon's cedars and Bashan's oaks fall, and the shepherds wail (11:1-3). Trees often stand for proud rulers in the prophets. The lament prepares for the failure of Israel's shepherds.

insights.title: An acted parable
insights.body: The prophet is told to shepherd the flock of slaughter (11:4), a flock exploited by buyers and sellers. This is one of the most obscure passages in the prophets, and scholars debate whether it describes real events, a symbolic drama, or a vision. The point is that God's people rejected the good shepherd he provided.

insights.title: Favor and Union
insights.body: The prophet takes two staffs named Favor and Union (11:7). Breaking Favor ends God's covenant protecting the flock from the nations (11:10). Breaking Union ends the brotherhood of Judah and Israel (11:14), the opposite of Ezekiel's sign of two sticks joined into one.

insights.title: Three shepherds in one month
insights.body: I cut off the three shepherds in one month (11:8) is one of the most debated verses in the Bible; scholars have proposed dozens of identifications from Israel's later kings to Maccabean-era high priests. No consensus exists. The point seems to be that God removed bad leaders, yet the flock still rejected the good shepherd.

insights.title: Thirty pieces of silver
insights.body: The shepherd's wage is thirty pieces of silver (11:12), the compensation set in the law for a slave killed by an ox. The handsome price (11:13) is sarcastic: it values the shepherd, and so God, at the price of a slave. He throws it to the potter in Yahweh's house.

insights.title: Judas's silver
insights.body: Matthew tells how Judas was paid thirty pieces of silver to betray Jesus, then threw the money into the temple, and the priests bought the potter's field. Matthew attributes the prophecy to Jeremiah, probably because he combines this passage with Jeremiah's purchase of a field and visit to the potter.

insights.title: The worthless shepherd
insights.body: Finally the prophet must act as a foolish shepherd who eats the fat sheep and tears off their hooves (11:16). The chapter ends with a curse on the worthless shepherd who deserts the flock (11:17). Jesus contrasts himself, the good shepherd, with the hired hand who abandons the sheep.

insights.title: Rejecting the good shepherd
insights.body: The flock loathed the shepherd who cared for them (11:8) and valued him at a slave's price. Why do people sometimes reject the leaders who serve them best, and prefer those who exploit them?

12.summary: Yahweh will make Jerusalem a cup of reeling and a heavy stone for the nations that attack it, will strengthen Judah, and will pour out a spirit of grace so that the people mourn bitterly for the one they have pierced.
12.lookfor: Notice the images for Jerusalem in 12:2-3, the order in which God saves Judah and Jerusalem, and who is pierced and mourned in 12:10.

names.name: Hadadrimmon
names.gloss: A place near Megiddo, or possibly a name for a storm god whose death was mourned.

names.name: Megiddon
names.gloss: Megiddo, a fortress city in the Jezreel valley where King Josiah was killed.

names.name: Nathan
names.gloss: Probably David's son Nathan, head of a branch of the royal family.

names.name: Shimeites
names.gloss: A Levite clan descended from Shimei, Levi's grandson.

insights.title: A cup of reeling
insights.body: Jerusalem becomes a cup of reeling (12:2), a drink that makes the nations stagger, an image the prophets use for God's judgment. It is also a burdensome stone that injures those who try to lift it (12:3). Weightlifting with heavy stones was a test of strength in the ancient world.

insights.title: Creator of the human spirit
insights.body: The oracle opens by describing Yahweh as the one who stretches out the heavens, lays the earth's foundation, and forms the spirit of man within him (12:1). The God who will defend Jerusalem is the Creator of everything. It also prepares for the spirit of grace poured out in 12:10.

insights.title: Judah first
insights.body: Yahweh will save the tents of Judah first, so that the glory of David's house and Jerusalem is not exalted over the countryside (12:7). The rural people and the capital are put on an equal footing. Even the feeblest will be like David (12:8).

insights.title: Whom they have pierced
insights.body: They will look to me whom they have pierced; and they shall mourn for him (12:10). The Hebrew moves from me to him, and interpreters debate who is pierced. John applies the verse to Jesus at the cross, and Revelation to his return. Some Jewish tradition in the Talmud applied it to a Messiah son of Joseph who would be slain.

insights.title: A spirit of grace and supplication
insights.body: God will pour out the spirit of grace and of supplication (12:10). Grace, hen, is God's favour; supplication is prayer for mercy. The mourning that follows is the result of God's gift, not human effort.

insights.title: Mourning for an only son
insights.body: They will mourn as for an only son or firstborn (12:10), the deepest grief in ancient Israel. The mourning of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddon (12:11) may recall the national lament for King Josiah, killed at Megiddo, or a ritual mourning for a dying god.

insights.title: Every family apart
insights.body: Each family mourns apart, and the men and women separately (12:12-14). The royal line of David and Nathan, and the priestly line of Levi and Shimei, are named. National repentance begins with leaders but reaches every household.

insights.title: Grief as a gift
insights.body: The spirit God pours out leads not first to joy but to mourning (12:10). Why might genuine grief over wrongdoing be a sign of grace rather than of judgment? Paul speaks of godly sorrow that leads to repentance.

13.summary: A fountain will be opened to cleanse Jerusalem from sin, idols and false prophets will vanish, and God's shepherd will be struck so that the sheep scatter and a refined third of the people remains.
13.lookfor: Notice the fountain in 13:1, how false prophets will act, and the poem about the struck shepherd in 13:7-9.

names.name: David
names.gloss: Israel's great king, whose house stands for the royal family.

insights.title: A fountain for sin
insights.body: A spring will be opened for David's house and Jerusalem for sin and uncleanness (13:1). It follows the mourning of chapter 12. Ezekiel promised that God would sprinkle clean water on his people, and the hymn There Is a Fountain Filled with Blood by William Cowper draws on this verse.

insights.title: The end of prophecy
insights.body: God will remove idols, false prophets and the spirit of impurity from the land (13:2). Anyone still claiming to prophesy will be disowned by his own parents (13:3), echoing the law against false prophets. Jewish tradition later held that prophecy had ceased after Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi.

insights.title: The hairy mantle
insights.body: False prophets will no longer wear a hairy mantle (13:4), the rough cloak that marked prophets such as Elijah. John the Baptist later wore camel's hair. The prophet's clothing had become a costume for deception.

insights.title: I am no prophet
insights.body: The false prophet will deny his calling: I am no prophet, I am a tiller of the ground (13:5), words that echo Amos's reply to Amaziah. Asked about wounds on his body, he will claim they came from friends (13:6). Ecstatic prophets sometimes cut themselves, so the wounds may betray him.

insights.title: Strike the shepherd
insights.body: Awake, sword, against my shepherd ... Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered (13:7). On the night of his arrest, Jesus quoted this verse to say his disciples would all desert him. The shepherd is called the man who is close to me, God's own associate.

insights.title: Wounds between your arms
insights.body: What are these wounds between your arms? (13:6). Because 13:7 follows directly, some Christian readers have linked the wounds to Christ's. In context, though, the speaker is a false prophet; most interpreters, including many Christians, read the verse that way.

insights.title: Refined like silver
insights.body: A third of the people will be brought through fire and refined like silver and gold (13:9). Then the covenant is renewed: They will call on my name, and I will hear them. I will say, It is my people. Suffering purifies rather than destroys the remnant.

insights.title: Scattered sheep
insights.body: Striking the shepherd scatters the sheep, yet God turns his hand to the little ones (13:7). Is this protection or further judgment? The Hebrew can be read either way. How can a scattering also be part of God's care?

14.summary: On the day of Yahweh the nations attack Jerusalem, but Yahweh stands on the Mount of Olives, splits it, and fights for his people; living waters flow from the city, Yahweh becomes king over all the earth, and everything in Jerusalem becomes holy.
14.lookfor: Notice the role of the Mount of Olives, the living waters, the confession in 14:9, and the bells of the horses in 14:20.

names.name: Mount of Olives
names.gloss: The ridge east of Jerusalem across the Kidron valley.

names.name: Azel
names.gloss: An unknown place, probably east of Jerusalem.

names.name: Uzziah
names.gloss: King of Judah in the 8th century BC, in whose reign a great earthquake struck.

names.name: Geba
names.gloss: A town in Benjamin marking Judah's northern border.

names.name: Rimmon
names.gloss: A town in the south of Judah.

names.name: tower of Hananel
names.gloss: A tower on Jerusalem's northern wall.

names.name: Canaanite
names.gloss: Here possibly a trader or merchant, since the word could mean both.

insights.title: The last battle
insights.body: All nations gather against Jerusalem and the city is partly taken (14:2), then Yahweh goes out to fight them (14:3). Zechariah 14 is a climax of the prophets' visions of a final battle. Interpreters read it literally of a future event, symbolically of God's final victory, or as a picture of the church's struggle.

insights.title: Feet on the Mount of Olives
insights.body: Yahweh's feet will stand on the Mount of Olives, and it will split in two (14:4). Ezekiel saw God's glory leave the temple and stand on this mountain. Jesus made his triumphal entry from the Mount of Olives and ascended from there; the angels in Acts say he will come back in the same way.

insights.title: The earthquake of Uzziah
insights.body: The people will flee as they fled from the earthquake in Uzziah's days (14:5), the same quake that dates Amos's book. It was remembered for more than two centuries. Archaeologists have found evidence of a major 8th-century BC earthquake at several sites.

insights.title: Living waters
insights.body: Living waters will flow from Jerusalem east to the Dead Sea and west to the Mediterranean, summer and winter (14:8). Most streams in the land dry up in summer. Ezekiel and Joel saw a river from the temple, and Revelation the river of the water of life.

insights.title: Yahweh will be one
insights.body: Yahweh will be King over all the earth. In that day Yahweh will be one, and his name one (14:9). It echoes the Shema, Hear Israel, Yahweh is one. Jewish worship closes the Aleinu prayer, recited at the end of every service, with this verse.

insights.title: A gruesome plague
insights.body: The nations that fought Jerusalem will rot where they stand (14:12). The image is horrifying and has troubled readers. Like other apocalyptic visions, it uses extreme language to say that those who attack God's people will not prevail.

insights.title: The feast of tents
insights.body: The surviving nations will go up every year to keep the feast of tents, or Tabernacles (14:16). It was the great autumn harvest festival and a time of prayer for rain, so nations that refuse will have no rain (14:17). Egypt, watered by the Nile rather than rain, gets its own warning.

insights.title: Holy to Yahweh on the horse bells
insights.body: Holy to Yahweh, once engraved on the high priest's turban, will be on the bells of horses, and every cooking pot will be as holy as the altar bowls (14:20-21). The line between sacred and ordinary disappears. What would it mean for everyday things to become holy? Jesus, driving traders from the temple, may have recalled the last line about no more Canaanite, or merchant, in Yahweh's house.

intro.who: Zechariah son of Berechiah, son of Iddo, a prophet and probably a priest who returned from Babylon, a contemporary of Haggai. Many scholars think chapters 9–14, which are undated and different in style, come from later disciples and are often called Second Zechariah; others defend single authorship.
intro.when: Chapters 1–8 are dated between 520 and 518 BC, during the rebuilding of the temple under Darius I. Chapters 9–14 are undated, and proposals range from the late 6th to the 4th century BC or later.
intro.why: It encourages the returned community to rebuild the temple and return to God through visions of God's renewed presence in Jerusalem, a purified priesthood and a coming king, and it looks ahead to a shepherd rejected, a city refined, and the day when Yahweh will be king over all the earth.
